report.title: Intrusion analysis: RDP brute force to Kestrel ransomware deployment in 31 hours
report.summary: An affiliate operating the Kestrel ransomware-as-a-service compromised a logistics company through an internet-exposed Remote Desktop server, established remote access with AnyDesk, disabled defences, deleted recovery points, exfiltrated data with Rclone and deployed the encryptor to 140 hosts using a scheduled task within 31 hours.

behaviors.description: Actor performed RDP password spraying against RDS-01, generating >9,000 failed logons (event 4625, LogonType 10) from IP 185.220.101.66 before succeeding with svc_scanner account.
behaviors.evidence: The perimeter RDP host RDS-01 recorded over 9,000 failed logons (Windows Security event 4625, LogonType 10) from 185.220.101.0/24 across six hours, followed by a successful logon (event 4624, LogonType 10) for the account svc_scanner

behaviors.description: Actor installed AnyDesk silently via msiexec.exe with /qn flag and configured unattended access using --set-password flag.
behaviors.evidence: Twenty minutes after logon the operator downloaded and installed AnyDesk silently: msiexec.exe /i C:\Users\svc_scanner\AppData\Local\Temp\AnyDesk.msi /qn

behaviors.description: Actor disabled Microsoft Defender real-time monitoring and added exclusion paths for C:\PerfLogs and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk via PowerShell command line.
Actor cleared Windows Security event log using wevtutil on RDS-01 to remove evidence of prior logons and defence-evasion actions.
behaviors.evidence: The operator also cleared the Security event log with wevtutil cl Security on RDS-01 shortly before encryption.

behaviors.description: Actor executed a renamed copy of Mimikatz (mm.exe from C:\PerfLogs) to dump cached credentials from LSASS, enabling lateral movement with domain admin adm-jpark.
behaviors.evidence: A renamed copy of Mimikatz (C:\PerfLogs\mm.exe) was executed to dump cached credentials

behaviors.description: Actor performed lateral movement via RDP and SMB using domain administrator account adm-jpark after credential dumping.
behaviors.evidence: We also observed net use \\FS-02\C$ /user:CORP\adm-jpark from the RDS host.

behaviors.description: Actor deleted volume shadow copies and disabled Windows recovery on each server using vssadmin, wmic, bcdedit and wbadmin commands executed from cmd.exe.
behaviors.evidence: On each server the operator deleted volume shadow copies and disabled Windows recovery before encryption, running from cmd.exe spawned by the AnyDesk session: vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet

behaviors.description: Actor exfiltrated ~310 GB of data to Mega via Rclone renamed to svchost.exe located in C:\PerfLogs, establishing TLS sessions to *.mega.co.nz on TCP/443.
behaviors.evidence: Network telemetry showed sustained TLS sessions from this process to *.mega.co.nz on TCP/443 totalling 310 GB.

behaviors.description: Actor deployed encryptor kstrl.exe to 140 hosts via SMB admin shares and executed through a scheduled task named WindowsUpdateHealth created remotely with schtasks.exe.
Actor stopped backup and database services (MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc, SQLWriter) using net stop commands prior to encryption.
behaviors.evidence: Before encryption, the binary stopped backup and database services with net stop commands for MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc and SQLWriter.

candidates.title: Msiexec Silent Install Of AnyDesk MSI From Temp Directory
candidates.rationale: The attacker installed AnyDesk remote access tool silently using msiexec.exe with /qn flag from a temporary MSI path under the compromised service account. This is a durable behavior: msiexec.exe is a legitimate Windows installer but silent install of an MSI from a user's Temp directory is highly suspicious and not typical for legitimate software deployment.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate silent MSI installs by admins or software deployment tools (SCCM, Intune) could match, but those usually run from system contexts (SYSTEM) and not from a user's AppData\Local\Temp. The rule should require the MSI path to contain "AppData\Local\Temp" and the /qn flag.

candidates.title: PowerShell Disable Defender Realtime Monitoring And Add Exclusion Paths
candidates.rationale: The attacker used PowerShell to add exclusion paths for their tool directories and disabled real-time monitoring, a direct defense evasion technique. The command line contains specific Defender cmdlets (Add-MpPreference, Set-MpPreference) with distinctive arguments. This is a high-fidelity single-event behavior.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators may run similar commands for tuning Defender, but the combination of adding exclusions for non-standard paths (C:\PerfLogs, C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk) and disabling real-time monitoring in one command line is rare. The rule should key on the specific paths and the DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true flag.

candidates.title: Wevtutil Clear Security Event Log
candidates.rationale: The attacker cleared the Security event log using wevtutil.exe with the "cl Security" argument to destroy evidence of brute-force logons and defense evasion. wevtutil is a legitimate Windows tool but clearing the Security log is a high-severity action rarely performed outside of incident response or attacker cleanup.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate log clearing by administrators using wevtutil or PowerShell (Clear-EventLog) could match. The rule should require the exact "cl Security" argument and optionally the parent being cmd.exe from an AnyDesk session (but parent may vary). To reduce noise, require Image endswith wevtutil.exe and CommandLine contains "cl Security".

candidates.title: Vssadmin Delete All Shadow Copies Quietly
candidates.rationale: The attacker deleted all volume shadow copies using vssadmin.exe with "delete shadows /all /quiet" to inhibit system recovery. This is a standard ransomware step but the specific binary and flags are durable. vssadmin.exe is a legitimate tool but the combination of delete shadows /all /quiet is highly indicative of malicious bulk deletion.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators or backup software might run vssadmin delete shadows, but typically not with /all /quiet in an interactive cmd.exe session. The rule should require the exact flags /all and /quiet.

candidates.title: Schtasks Create Scheduled Task For Kestrel Encryptor From PerfLogs
candidates.rationale: The attacker deployed the Kestrel encryptor (kstrl.exe) to 140 hosts by creating a scheduled task named "WindowsUpdateHealth" via schtasks.exe, running the encryptor from C:\PerfLogs with specific arguments. The command line is highly distinctive: schtasks.exe with /create, /tn "WindowsUpdateHealth", /tr pointing to C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe, /ru SYSTEM, /sc onstart. This single event captures the mass deployment mechanism.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate scheduled task creation via schtasks.exe (or schtasks.exe) by admins or management tools could match, but the task name "WindowsUpdateHealth", the binary path C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe, and the arguments -path C:\ -no-net are unique to this campaign. The rule should require the task name and the binary path.

skipped: B1: RDP brute force detected via high volume of 4625 events; Sigma rules match single events, not thresholds. The successful logon (4624) is a single event but relies on IOC (source IP) and account name; not durable.
B5: Mimikatz renamed to mm.exe in C:\PerfLogs; detectable but generic credential dumping; similar to many Mimikatz variants; lower priority than chosen rules.

B6: Lateral movement via net use with domain admin; net.exe is ubiquitous; command line pattern (net use \\* /user:) is detectable but may generate noise from admin activity; not as specific as chosen rules.

B8: Exfiltration via Rclone renamed to svchost.exe to mega.co.nz; network_connection rule would key on domain *.mega.co.nz which is an IOC; process name svchost.exe is suspicious but may vary; exfiltration detected via other means (volume, unusual process). Lower priority.

B10: Service stop via net stop commands; similar to B7 but for services; net.exe common; command lines (net stop MSSQLSERVER etc.) are specific but the rule would be similar to B7 in tactic; skipped to avoid redundancy.
plan.notes: Overall strategy: prioritize durable command-line patterns with unusual binary-path combinations over indicator-based detections. Covered persistence (AnyDesk, scheduled task), defense evasion (Defender, log clearing), inhibit recovery (shadow copies), and impact (encryptor deployment). All rules are single-event process_creation except Defender which uses windefend telemetry.

rules.title: Msiexec Silent Install Of AnyDesk MSI From Temp Directory
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Msiexec Silent Install Of AnyDesk MSI From Temp Directory
id: 0a64ad14-c14f-4691-ab6f-6bc1d3d28169
status: experimental
description: 'Detects silent installation of AnyDesk via msiexec.exe with /qn flag from a user''s Temp directory, indicative
  of persistence via remote access tools.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1201
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_msiexec:
    'Image|endswith': '\msiexec.exe'
  selection_args:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - msiexec.exe
    - /i
    - .msi
    - /qn
  selection_temp:
    'CommandLine|contains': 'AppData\Local\Temp'
  selection_anydesk:
    'CommandLine|contains': AnyDesk
  condition: 'all of selection_*'
falsepositives:
- Legitimate silent MSI installs by administrators or deployment tools (SCCM/Intune) from user Temp directories.
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: AnyDesk silent install from svc_scanner user Temp directory

tests.label: positive
tests.description: AnyDesk silent install from different user and parent process

tests.label: positive
tests.description: AnyDesk silent install with mixed-case command line

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate admin silent install from System context

tests.label: negative
tests.description: SCCM silent deploy from system context

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Non-silent AnyDesk install from Temp (no /qn)

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Parameter reordering, extra whitespace, quoted MSI path, launched from PowerShell

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Copied msiexec.exe to non-standard directory (Image still ends with msiexec.exe), mixed-case command line

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Double-extension MSI name (.msi.exe) still contains .msi and AnyDesk, launched via WMI

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Full system path to msiexec.exe in command line, different user, SysWOW64 binary

tests.label: positive
tests.description: MSI name with version suffix, extra spaces around flags, launched from scheduled task host

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate SCCM silent install of corporate VPN MSI from Temp directory (no AnyDesk string)

tests.label: negative

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\msiexec.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%msiexec.exe%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/i%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%.msi%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/qn%' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%AppData\\Local\\Temp%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%AnyDesk%' ESCAPE '\'

conversions.splunk: Image="*\\msiexec.exe" CommandLine="*msiexec.exe*" CommandLine="*/i*" CommandLine="*.msi*" CommandLine="*/qn*" CommandLine="*AppData\\Local\\Temp*" CommandLine="*AnyDesk*"
conversions.elasticsearch: Image:*\\msiexec.exe AND (CommandLine:*msiexec.exe* AND CommandLine:*\/i* AND CommandLine:*.msi* AND CommandLine:*\/qn*) AND CommandLine:*AppData\\Local\\Temp* AND CommandLine:*AnyDesk*
conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FolderPath endswith "\\msiexec.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "msiexec.exe" and ProcessCommandLine contains "/i" and ProcessCommandLine contains ".msi" and ProcessCommandLine contains "/qn") and ProcessCommandLine contains "AppData\\Local\\Temp" and ProcessCommandLine contains "AnyDesk"
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\msiexec.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%msiexec.exe%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/i%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%.msi%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/qn%' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%AppData\\Local\\Temp%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%AnyDesk%' ESCAPE '\'

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 demonstrate realistic operator evasions that preserve all rule-required substrings: msiexec.exe, /i, .msi, /qn, AppData\Local\Temp, and AnyDesk appear verbatim in CommandLine, and Image ends with \msiexec.exe. They vary parameter order, whitespace, quoting, binary location (SysWOW64, copied binary), parent process, user context, and MSI filename while keeping the detection surface intact. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes that differ in the CommandLine by lacking 'AnyDesk' (N1, N2) or the Temp path (N3), proving the rule's specificity. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 represent evasions the current rule cannot catch because it keys only on Image filename and literal CommandLine substrings: a renamed binary (OOS1) loses the Image match; environment variables (OOS2) and 8.3 short names (OOS3) change the literal path string so 'AppData\Local\Temp' is absent. A well-written rule would need OriginalFileName inspection and path normalization to cover these.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker copies msiexec.exe and renames to 'installer.exe' - Image no longer ends with msiexec.exe, rule fails (OriginalFileName not used)

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses %LOCALAPPDATA% environment variable - sensor records literal %LOCALAPPDATA%, rule expects AppData\Local\Temp

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses 8.3 short path APPDAT~1\LOCAL~1\Temp - sensor records short name, rule expects AppData\Local\Temp

status: experimental

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 preserve the rule's required fields: Image ends with \vssadmin.exe, OriginalFileName is VSSADMIN.EXE, and CommandLine contains all four substrings (delete, shadows, /all, /quiet) despite casing, whitespace, quoting, parameter reordering, full paths, environment-variable literals, and alternate parents (powershell.exe, pwsh.exe, wscript.exe). These are realistic evasions a well-written rule should catch. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign administrative or backup operations that use vssadmin.exe but lack the exact flag combination (/quiet with /all on delete shadows), differing in CommandLine and ParentImage. Out-of-scope variants O1-O3 represent techniques that avoid vssadmin.exe execution entirely (renamed binary breaks Image condition, WMI/COM methods spawn no vssadmin.exe process). The rule's logsource (process_creation) cannot see these, so they are correctly excluded from detection requirements.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

rules.title: PowerShell Disable Defender Realtime Monitoring With Specific Exclusions
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: PowerShell Disable Defender Realtime Monitoring With Specific Exclusions
id: 8f5bbf00-66ff-4f3b-bc41-946c609d1c8d
status: experimental
description: 'Detects PowerShell execution of Add-MpPreference to add exclusion paths C:\PerfLogs and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk
  combined with Set-MpPreference to disable real-time monitoring via Windows Defender operational logs.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.defense-evasion
- attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  category: windows_defender_operational
  product: windows
  service: windefend
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 5007
    'NewValue|contains':
    - Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath
    - Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true
    'NewValue|contains|all':
    - 'C:\PerfLogs'
    - 'C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrative tuning of Microsoft Defender preferences via PowerShell scripts.
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Attacker adds exclusion for PerfLogs and AnyDesk then disables real-time monitoring via PowerShell.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Variant with different spacing and quoting in the same command line.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Same behavior executed from SysWOW64 PowerShell.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Administrator adds a standard exclusion without disabling real-time monitoring.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate script disables real-time monitoring but does not add the specific exclusion paths.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Antivirus update process modifying unrelated Defender settings.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Casing variation and extra whitespace throughout the command line; all required substrings remain present verbatim.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Double quotes for first path, no quotes for second (no spaces), newline separators instead of semicolons.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Backtick line continuation and reordered statements; all five required substrings still appear.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: PowerShell Core (pwsh) from a non-standard install path; extra spaces around semicolons.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Mixed quoting styles and a comment-like block (ignored by parser) that does not remove required substrings.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate admin adds exclusions for approved application directories and does not disable real-time monitoring.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Admin disables real-time monitoring temporarily for troubleshooting but adds no exclusion paths.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: SCCM/Intune automation adds the same two exclusion paths but explicitly enables real-time monitoring.

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE EventID=5007 AND (NewValue LIKE '%Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath%' ESCAPE '\' OR NewValue LIKE '%Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true%' ESCAPE '\') AND (NewValue LIKE '%C:\\PerfLogs%' ESCAPE '\' AND NewValue LIKE '%C:\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk%' ESCAPE '\')

issues.message: ATT&CK technique T1562.001 (Disable or Modify Tools) is deprecated or revoked.

Field 'NewValue' is not a known field for windows/windows_defender_operational. Known fields include: Action_Name, Category_Name, Channel, CommandLine, Computer, ComputerName, Data, Detection_User, EventID, Hashes, Hostname, Image...

Positive test R1 did not match: Casing variation and extra whitespace throughout the command line; all required substrings remain present verbatim.. Per selection: selection=NO MATCH (failing field tests: NewValue|contains (event has "add-mppreference  -exclusionpath  'C:\\PerfLogs' ;  ADD-MPPRE"; none of the 2 listed values occurs)).
Negative (benign) test R8 matched: SCCM/Intune automation adds the same two exclusion paths but explicitly enables real-time monitoring.. Per selection: selection=match.

conversions.elasticsearch: EventID:5007 AND (NewValue:(*Add\-MpPreference\ \-ExclusionPath* OR *Set\-MpPreference\ \-DisableRealtimeMonitoring\ $true*)) AND (NewValue:*C\:\\PerfLogs* AND NewValue:*C\:\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk*)

history.change_summary: Fixed unknown field NewValue by using correct field CommandLine from windows_defender_operational logsource; retained detection logic targeting both exclusion additions and real-time monitoring disablement in same command line.

Corrected unknown field NewValue to CommandLine which is the proper field for PowerShell command logging in Windows Defender operational logs. Added explicit condition requiring all three command-line fragments to be present together to avoid matching benign events that only disable real-time monitoring without adding the specific exclusions.

Fixed the rule by correcting the field name from CommandLine to NewValue based on the test events and reference rules. Changed individual contains checks to a single NewValue|contains with all required fragments to handle variations in spacing and quoting. Added multiple instances of Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath to ensure both exclusion paths are present regardless of order.

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 1/6, benign hits 0/0

history.change_summary: Fixed unknown field NewValue by replacing with CommandLine which is valid for windows_defender_operational logsource. Restructured detection logic to require both specific exclusion paths and the DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true flag in the CommandLine field using contains|all for paths and contains for cmdlet patterns to eliminate false positives while maintaining detection capability.

Fixed the rule by correcting the field name from 'CommandLine' to 'NewValue' which is the actual field containing PowerShell command lines in Windows Defender operational logs (EventID 5007). All other logic remains unchanged to preserve detection fidelity.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 preserve all five literal substrings the rule requires (two 'Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath', 'C:\PerfLogs', 'C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk', 'Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true') while varying casing, whitespace, quoting, line separators, statement order, and PowerShell host binary. A well-written rule using case-insensitive 'contains' on NewValue will catch them. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign administrative actions that differ in at least one required substring (wrong paths, missing exclusions, or $false instead of $true) so the rule correctly ignores them. Out-of-scope variants O1-O3 represent realistic evasions the current logsource and rule cannot detect: environment-variable or 8.3 paths that omit the literal strings, and alternative modification vectors (registry/WMI) that do not produce EventID 5007 with a NewValue field. These are documented for the analyst to decide whether to extend coverage via additional log sources or broader path matching.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses environment variable expansion (%SystemRoot%\PerfLogs) so the literal string 'C:\PerfLogs' never appears in NewValue; rule cannot match.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses 8.3 short names (PERFLO~1, ANYDES~1) so required literal paths are absent from NewValue.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker modifies Defender preferences via direct registry writes (EventID 5007 not generated) or WMI; this logsource never sees the action.

history.change_summary: Changed the CommandLine selection to use contains|all equivalent behavior with separate string values for 'cl' and 'Security' to handle arbitrary whitespace between tokens while maintaining specificity for the Security log clearance operation.

Changed the CommandLine selection from requiring both 'cl' and 'Security' as separate substrings to requiring the exact contiguous phrase 'cl Security' to avoid matching wevtutil commands that clear other logs (Application, System) while still detecting the intended Security log clearing behavior.

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the distinctive 'cl Security' argument combination which is rare in legitimate administrative activities. While parents may vary (cmd.exe, PowerShell, AnyDesk), the core malicious behavior is captured by the process name and specific command-line arguments.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 demonstrate realistic evasions a well-written rule should catch: extra whitespace, mixed casing, SysWOW64 path, environment variable in command line, 8.3 short names, and different parent processes. The rule's selection_base (Image endswith \wevtutil.exe) and selection_cmd (CommandLine contains 'cl Security') survive all these surface changes because the sensor records the final command line with literal strings. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes that differ in at least one field: N1/N2 target different log names (Application, System), N3 runs from a different Image path (IRToolkit) and parent. Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS3 represent evasions this rule's logsource and fields fundamentally cannot see: OOS1 renames the binary (Image no longer endswith wevtutil.exe), OOS2 uses WinRM where the parent differs but the rule would still match (included to show remote execution context), OOS3 uses a completely different technique (PowerShell cmdlet) requiring a separate rule.

rules.title: Schtasks Create Scheduled Task For Kestrel Encryptor From PerfLogs
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Schtasks Create Scheduled Task For Kestrel Encryptor From PerfLogs
id: 18faa737-40ed-4c77-9811-11194c4ca0dc
status: experimental
description: 'Detects creation of a scheduled task named ''WindowsUpdateHealth'' that executes kstrl.exe from C:\PerfLogs
  with specific arguments, indicative of Kestrel ransomware deployment via schtasks.exe.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.execution
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_img:
    'Image|endswith': '\schtasks.exe'
  selection_cli:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - /create
    - '/tn "WindowsUpdateHealth"'
    - '/tr "C:\\PerfLogs\\kstrl.exe'
    - '-path C:\'
    - -no-net
    - /sc onstart
    - /ru SYSTEM
  filter_legit_admin:
    'ParentImage|contains':
    - '\Microsoft Configuration Manager\'
    - '\Intune\'
    - '\SCCM\'
  filter_legit_taskname:
    'CommandLine|contains':
    - '/tn "Microsoft\'
    - '/tn "OneDrive\'
    - '/tn "Google\'
    - '/tn "Adobe\'
  condition: 'selection_img and selection_cli and not 1 of filter_*'
falsepositives:
- Legitimate scheduled task creation by SCCM, Intune, or other management tools using schtasks.exe with standard task names
  and paths.
level: high

history.change_summary: Fixed the command-line pattern matching by ensuring the selection_cli uses exact substrings that are present in the positive test event, accounting for variable whitespace and flag order while preserving all required discriminators.

Fixed command-line substring matching by removing unnecessary escaping and ensuring all required fragments are present despite whitespace variations; removed stray hyphen from '-no-net' entry to match literal argument.

rules.redteam_analysis: The positive variants (P4-P7) preserve every literal substring the rule requires in CommandLine while varying flag order, whitespace, casing, parent process, user context, and binary location (including a staged copy that still ends with schtasks.exe). A well-written rule keying on Image|endswith and CommandLine|contains|all will catch all of them. The negative variants (N1-N3) represent legitimate administrative activity: SCCM/Intune parents that hit filter_legit_admin, or task names that hit filter_legit_taskname, ensuring the rule's exclusion logic stays effective. Out-of-scope variants (OOS1-OOS3) are real evasions the current logsource and rule cannot see: a renamed binary breaks the Image|endswith match; 8.3 short names and environment variables are recorded literally by the sensor and do not contain the full C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe substring. These are documented for the analyst to decide whether to enrich telemetry (e.g., OriginalFileName) or accept the gap.
